summary: In situ OAM (IOAM) records telemetry data in packets as they travel along a path. This document describes how to carry IOAM data fields inside the Network Service Header (NSH), which is used for service function chaining. It covers the encapsulation only, not new measurements.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine each stop on a bus route stamps your ticket as you pass. This document says where on the ticket the stamps go when the ticket is a service-chain envelope.

questions: carry telemetry in network service header
how does ioam work with service function chaining
subtitle: Where in a Network Service Header packet the in situ OAM telemetry data goes.

tldr.problem: In situ OAM (IOAM) records telemetry inside data packets as they cross a network, but there was no defined way to carry it in the Network Service Header (NSH) used for service function chaining.
tldr.mechanism: A new NSH Next Protocol value, 0x06, marks an IOAM header that follows the NSH headers. The header holds an IOAM-Type, a length, a reserved byte and a Next Protocol field, followed by the IOAM data.
tldr.outcome: IOAM data can ride in NSH packets, and several IOAM option types can be stacked. Nodes that do not support the IOAM header SHOULD drop such packets.

today: RFC 9452 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2023 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines only the NSH encapsulation of IOAM data; the data fields themselves come from RFC 9197.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
IOAM (In situ Operations, Administration, and Maintenance), defined in RFC 9197, records OAM information while a packet crosses a network domain. The words in situ mean the data is added to the data packets themselves, rather than sent in packets dedicated to OAM.

RFC 9452 defines how the IOAM-Data-Fields are carried in the Network Service Header (NSH, RFC 8300) for the Service Function Chaining architecture (RFC 7665). It covers the encapsulation only.
sections.plainLanguage: Some packets carry little notes about their trip. This document says where to tuck the notes when the packet travels in a special service-chain envelope.

sections.title: The IOAM Header in NSH
sections.content:
IOAM-Data-Fields are carried as NSH payload. A Next Protocol header follows the NSH headers, and an IOAM header with the data is added. The NSH Next Protocol value is 0x06. The fields are:

  • IOAM-Type: 8 bits, the IOAM Option-Type from the registry in RFC 9197.
  • IOAM HDR Len: 8 bits, the header length in multiples of 4 octets, including the IOAM-Type and IOAM HDR Len fields.
  • Reserved bits: MUST be set to 0x0 when sent and ignored when received.
  • Next Protocol: 8 bits, the type of header that follows IOAM, with the same meaning as in RFC 8300.
  • IOAM Option and Optional Data Space: the IOAM-Data-Fields for that type, always aligned to 4 octets, so there is no padding field.

The O bit MUST be handled following the rules in RFC 9451.
sections.plainLanguage: The IOAM label says what kind of notes are inside, how long the notes are, and what comes after them. The notes always fit neatly in 4-byte chunks.

sections.title: Handling in the Network
sections.content:
In a domain that uses IOAM, inserting the IOAM header is enabled at the NSH tunnel endpoints, which are also configured as encapsulating and decapsulating nodes for IOAM. The operator MUST ensure that SFC-aware nodes along the Service Function Path support IOAM, or packets might be dropped. IOAM transit nodes, such as a Service Function Forwarder, MUST process all IOAM headers that are relevant under their configuration.

Multiple IOAM Option-Types MAY appear in one NSH encapsulation. With two of them before the payload, the Next Protocol of the first holds 0x06 and that of the second names the payload type. If the Incremental Trace Option-Type is used, a transit node adjusts IOAM HDR Len to match.

A node that does not support the IOAM header SHOULD drop the packet, following RFC 8300. How such events are maintained or reported is out of scope. The IOAM Active and Loopback flags (RFC 9322) are also out of scope for now.
sections.plainLanguage: Only the entrances and exits of the route add and remove the stamps, and every stop in the middle has to know how to read them. A stop that cannot read them should throw the ticket away.

sections.title: Why This Encapsulation Was Chosen
sections.content:
The appendix compares three approaches. The first would use NSH MD Type 2 with a type per IOAM option. The second would give each IOAM Option-Type its own Next Protocol value. The third, chosen here, allocates a single Next Protocol code point for IOAM and uses a sub-type field to say which option type is carried.

The goals were an encapsulation friendly to hardware and software forwarders and room for large deployments. Hardware prefers flat TLV structures over nested ones, so the trace, proof-of-transit and edge-to-edge options are carried as a serial sequence. The chosen option avoids an extra layer of TLV nesting and, unlike NSH MD Type 2, does not limit IOAM data to a maximum of 256 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors tried three ways to pack the notes and picked the one that is simple for fast machines to read and has no small size limit.

sections.title: IANA Allocation
sections.content: IANA allocated one code point in the NSH Next Protocol registry: 0x06, meaning the Next Protocol is an IOAM header, with RFC 9452 as the reference.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of envelope types now has an entry that means IOAM notes come next.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: IOAM is a per-domain feature: the operator decides how to use and configure it. The operator needs to properly secure the IOAM domain to avoid malicious configuration and use, which could include injecting malicious IOAM packets into the domain. For more, the RFC points to Section 9 of RFC 9197 and Section 5 of RFC 9451.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the notes are inside real packets, the network owner must keep strangers from slipping in fake notes.
